title: Explainable AI for Diabetic Retinopathy Screening in Rural India
dataset_link: APTOS 2019 Blindness Detection: https://www.kaggle.com/c/aptos2019- blindness-detection IDRiD (Indian Diabetic Retinopathy Image Dataset): https://ieeedataport.org/open-access/indian-diabetic-retinopathy-image-dataset-idrid DRIVE (Vessel Extraction): https://drive.grand-challenge.org/ Messidor-2: https://www.adcis.net/en/third-party/messidor2/
description:
Background:
India has over 77 million diabetic adults - the second highest globally. Diabetic Retinopathy (DR) affects ~18% of this population and is a leading cause of preventable blindness. Early screening can prevent90% of vision loss, but India has only ~1 ophthalmologist per 100,000 rural population, making mass manual screening infeasible. Existing AI solutions function as black boxes, lack clinical validation rigor, and fail with variable image quality from portable fundus cameras in field conditions. A robust, explainable, and validated screening system is essential for deployment in primary healthcare centres across rural India.
Description:
Design a MATLAB-based retinal image analysis pipeline for automated DR screening addressing real-world deployment challenges:
1. Image Quality Assessment and Enhancement: Automatically evaluate fundus images for adequacy (focus, illumination, field of view). Apply adaptive enhancement (CLAHE, illumination normalization, denoising) for borderline images; reject ungradeable ones with recapture feedback.
2. Retinal Structure Segmentation: Extract clinically relevant structures - optic disc/fovea localization, vessel segmentation, microaneurysm detection, exudate segmentation, hemorrhage classification, and neovascularization detection.
3. DR Severity Grading: Classify using the International Clinical DR severity scale (Levels 0-4, from no DR to proliferative DR) with clinically acceptable sensitivity (>90%) and specificity (>85%) for referable DR (Level 2+).
4. Explainability Module: Implement Grad-CAM attention maps, lesion-level evidence correlated with clinical criteria, calibrated confidence scores, and automated annotated reports - enabling ophthalmologist validation in under 30 seconds for a human-in-theloop workflow.
5. Simulink Workflow Simulation: Model the telemedicine screening pipeline in Simulink - image acquisition rates, bandwidth constraints, processing throughput, and review capacity - to optimize resource allocation for district-level programs serving 100,000+ patients annually.
This problem demands clinical validation rigor, sub-pixel microaneurysm detection, and clinically meaningful explainability
• Tools: Image Processing Toolbox, Computer Vision Toolbox, Deep Learning Toolbox, Medical Imaging Toolbox, Simulink, Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox Expected Solution: A working prototype demonstrating: DR classification with >90% sensitivity and >85% specificity for referable DR;
explainable Grad-CAM outputs rated as clinically useful; a Simulink model optimizing screening resource allocation; and validation against published benchmarks showing the integrated pipeline outperforms any single technique approach.
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on ai, machine learning, deep learning applied to a clean & green technology problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (5/5): reaches a broad public/citizen base within Clean & Green Technology. Tech Depth (3/5): centers on model. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (3/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 22/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: Explainable AI for Diabetic Retinopathy Screening in Rural India

overview.in_plain_terms: Build an AI system that screens retinal images for diabetic eye disease and explains its reasoning clearly, so it can work reliably in rural clinics where there's no ophthalmologist to double-check, and where the person operating it needs to trust and understand the result.
overview.why_it_matters: India has millions of diabetics and almost no rural ophthalmologists. A trustworthy, explainable screening tool is the difference between preventable blindness being caught early or not caught at all.
pain_points: India has roughly 1 ophthalmologist per 100,000 rural population, mass manual screening is infeasible.
Existing AI solutions are black boxes with limited clinical validation.
Field conditions (portable fundus cameras, variable image quality) break many existing models.
overview.background: Diabetic Retinopathy affects a significant share of India's large diabetic population and is a leading cause of preventable blindness, but rural ophthalmologist scarcity makes manual screening infeasible at scale, and existing AI tools lack the explainability and field-robustness needed for real deployment.
overview.whats_being_asked: A MATLAB-based retinal image analysis pipeline for DR screening: image quality assessment/enhancement, retinal structure segmentation (optic disc, vessels, microaneurysms, exudates, hemorrhages, neovascularization), built for explainability and field-condition robustness.
expected_solution: Automated image quality assessment with enhancement or rejection of ungradeable images.
Segmentation of clinically relevant retinal structures.
Explainable classification output, not a black-box score.
Robustness to variable field-condition image quality.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough. This isn't just DR classification (a well-trodden category), it specifically demands explainability and field-robustness, the two things existing solutions are explicitly criticized for lacking, that's the genuinely hard, differentiating part.
analysis.invention_effort_note: Moderate. MATLAB provides strong built-in medical image processing and segmentation tooling, which meaningfully reduces the from-scratch engineering burden compared to building this in a general-purpose language.

competitive_landscape.note: DR screening is a recognizable medical-AI hackathon category, but the explicit explainability and field-robustness requirements narrow the field to teams willing to go beyond a basic classifier.

innovation.note: Explainability and field-robustness are the genuinely hard, under-solved parts of this problem, not classification accuracy alone.

invention.note: MATLAB's built-in medical imaging toolset significantly eases the segmentation/analysis pipeline build.

technical_feasibility.note: Public retinal image datasets exist for training/testing (e.g. established DR research datasets), reducing data-sourcing risk.

impact_and_benefits.note: Preventable blindness at scale for an underserved rural population, an unusually concrete and severe impact case.

architecture.note: Image quality assessment, segmentation, classification, and explanation generation form a clear, linear pipeline.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick, one of the more genuinely well-resourced PS in the batch (public datasets exist, strong tooling available via MATLAB) while still being technically substantial and high-impact. The explainability requirement is what separates a strong submission from a generic classifier.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Public retinal image datasets exist for real training/testing, a genuine data-sourcing advantage relative to most PS in this batch.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Building 'just another DR classifier' without genuinely addressing explainability (why did the model flag this image, which specific structures triggered it) misses the actual differentiating ask in the PS.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Commit real build time specifically to the explainability output (highlighting which detected structures, e.g. specific microaneurysms or hemorrhages, drove the classification), not just an accuracy number.

idea_0_4: Source a public DR image dataset for training/testing (several established research datasets exist).
Design your explainability approach upfront: structure-level highlighting (showing detected microaneurysms/exudates/hemorrhages on the image) is more clinically useful than a generic saliency map.
Split: one person on the image quality/segmentation pipeline, one on classification and explainability output.
prototype_4_22: Build the image quality assessment and enhancement step (reject genuinely ungradeable images rather than forcing a low-confidence classification).
Build the retinal structure segmentation (start with the most clinically critical: microaneurysms and hemorrhages).
Start the classification layer, tied directly to the segmented structures, not a separate black-box model.
integration_22_30: Connect quality assessment -> segmentation -> classification -> explainable output end to end.
Test specifically with lower-quality, field-condition-style images, not just clean dataset samples, this directly addresses the PS's stated real-world gap.
Build the explanation visualization: highlighted structures overlaid on the original image with the classification reasoning.
polish_30_36: Polish the explanation output for clinical usability, a rural health worker needs to understand it quickly, not a data scientist.
Rehearse walking through a real screening case end to end: image in, quality check, structures highlighted, classification with visible reasoning.
Prepare to discuss validation rigor honestly, what real clinical validation this would need before deployment.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Show the explainability output on a real borderline case, where the model's confidence is moderate, not a clean obvious example, and walk through exactly which detected structures drove the classification, that's what proves genuine explainability, not just accuracy.

strengths: Public datasets genuinely available, reducing data-sourcing risk relative to most PS in this batch.
MATLAB's medical imaging toolset meaningfully eases the technical build.
weaknesses: Explainability is genuinely harder to build well than raw classification accuracy, easy to under-invest in it.
Field-condition robustness (the PS's other key ask) requires deliberately testing against degraded images, not just clean dataset samples.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: CV/medical-imaging-weighted, ideally with someone comfortable in MATLAB given the PS's framing.
team_fit.approach: Research actual clinical DR grading criteria (what specific findings indicate each severity level) before building, this grounds both classification and explainability in real medical logic.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard image preprocessing and segmentation using MATLAB's medical imaging toolbox, well-supported patterns.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Designing explanations that are actually clinically meaningful (which structures matter, how to present them to a non-specialist health worker), that's domain and UX judgment together.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: A black-box classifier dressed up with a generic 'explanation' visualization (like an unstructured saliency heatmap) doesn't actually solve the explainability gap the PS specifically calls out, it needs to be clinically grounded, structure-level explanation.

data_resource_availability.status: Public retinal image datasets for DR research do exist and are accessible, a genuine data advantage for this PS.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: If field-condition-quality images specifically (portable fundus camera style) aren't available, simulate degraded quality by applying realistic noise/blur/illumination variation to clean dataset images, and label this clearly as simulated field conditions.

judge_qna.question: What makes your explanation actually clinically meaningful, versus a generic AI explainability technique?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Point to the specific detected structures (microaneurysms, exudates, hemorrhages) your explanation highlights, tied to actual clinical DR grading criteria, not a generic saliency map that a health worker couldn't interpret.
judge_qna.follow_up: Has this explanation format been validated with any actual healthcare worker, even informally?

judge_qna.question: How does your system perform on genuinely poor-quality field images, not clean dataset samples?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Show your results on deliberately degraded test images, and describe your rejection mechanism for genuinely ungradeable images, being honest about where quality assessment draws that line.
judge_qna.follow_up: What happens to a patient whose image gets rejected as ungradeable, what's the fallback?
